items.prompt: State what is meant by the term outputs in an industrial system.
items.canonical_answer: The outputs of an industrial system are what comes out of it: the products the system makes and sells, and the waste it creates while making them, such as chimney gases, waste water and solid offcuts.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the meaning: outputs are what comes out of the system, and the term covers both products and waste - naming either one alone is incomplete.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how the inputs of a sawmill are turned into its outputs.
items.canonical_answer: Inputs such as logs, blades and machines, power and the sawyers' labour are used by the processes: the logs are debarked, cut into planks, planed and seasoned, which turns one raw material into a new product. The processes release the outputs: sawn planks for sale, and waste - sawdust, bark and offcuts - because cutting strips away material the product does not use, so part of every log leaves as waste.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: inputs named (logs, energy, labour) taken up by the processes; how the processes change the material, because the change is what makes it processing; so the outputs include products and waste together.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows the approximate annual flows of a fish cannery, in tonnes:

| flow | tonnes a year |
|---|---|
| whole fish landed | 40 000 |
| canned fish sold | 32 000 |
| waste to fishmeal | 8 000 |

Describe what the flows show about the cannery as an industrial system.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the system in balance: the 40 000 tonnes of fish that enter as an input leave again, as 32 000 tonnes of product and 8 000 tonnes of waste, 32 000 + 8 000 = 40 000. The product is the larger output stream: 32 000 / 40 000 = 0.8, so four fifths of the intake by mass becomes canned fish, and 8 000 / 40 000 = 0.2, so one fifth becomes waste. The figures mean the cannery turns most of its raw material into product rather than discarding it, which is why the waste is worth selling to a fishmeal plant instead of dumping.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - what enters equals what leaves, split between product and waste (1 mark).

Values: the shares worked from the figures - 0.8 of the intake becomes product, 0.2 becomes waste - so the figures support the words (1 mark); the balance of the system stated, which means the table is read as a whole (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A brickworks is planned at a site with a clay pit beside it, a main road 1 kilometre away, mains electricity at the site, and a town of 20 000 people 5 kilometres away. Suggest two inputs the brickworks will draw from the town and one input it will draw from elsewhere, giving a reason for each.
items.canonical_answer: Labour: the town's 20 000 people hold the workers the works needs, because moulding, firing and packing all take hands. Water: the town's mains can supply the works, because brickmaking mixes clay with water, so a nearby network spares the works its own borehole. From elsewhere, clay: the pit beside the site provides the raw material, because the clay travels a short hop onto the site rather than by road.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per input with its reason, 3 in all, each tied to this example - labour and water from the town, clay from the pit.
Each reason must follow from the figure given, because an input named without its source suggests nothing about location.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Asked to sort a cannery's flows, a learner writes: "Inputs: the tins of fish ready for sale. Processes: the processing of the fish. Outputs: the fish that arrive at the quay." Explain the two errors.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has swapped inputs and outputs: the tins ready for sale come out of the factory, so they are outputs, and the fish arriving at the quay go in, so they are inputs. The learner has also defined the processes by repeating the word, which explains nothing - processing is the change that turns raw material into a new product, here cleaning, cooking and canning the fish. The test for any flow: does it go into the factory, or come out?
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the first error - inputs and outputs are confused, and in fact the two flows belong the other way round.
1 mark: the second error - repeating the word "processing" is not a definition; the correct idea is that processing changes a raw material into a new product.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A cannery sends 8 000 tonnes of trimmings a year to a fishmeal plant instead of dumping them, but its chimneys release the same waste gases as before. Suggest how far the manager is right to say the factory is now a clean system.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is partly right. One output has been improved: solid waste no longer leaves the system as dumped material, because the trimmings become another plant's input, which is a real gain. But the system as a whole still releases its waste gases, and since gases are outputs too, the evidence of the two streams shows an improved system rather than a clean one. The better judgement is that the factory has closed part of the loop while its gaseous outputs remain, so calling it clean overstates the change.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision on how far the claim holds (1 mark).
Because the evidence is weighed: solid waste improved, gaseous outputs unchanged, since both are outputs of the system (1 mark).
So the judgement is refined against the figures of the two output streams rather than accepted or rejected flat (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two factors that influence where a factory is located.
items.canonical_answer: Raw materials: bulk-losing industries such as cement locate beside the quarry, because hauling rock costs more than hauling the cement it becomes. Markets: perishable or bulky products such as bread are made near the buyers, so bakeries sit in towns rather than beside the flour mill.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: any two location factors (raw materials, labour, energy, transport, markets, land, government policy), and each fact given must be a location factor, not an impact of the factory.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why a sugar mill is usually built beside the cane fields rather than in the distant city where the sugar is eaten.
items.canonical_answer: Sugar milling is bulk-losing: roughly seven tonnes of cane become one tonne of sugar, because the fibre and water are squeezed out at the mill. So a mill beside the fields hauls a small refined product the long distance, while a mill in the city would haul seven times as much raw cane, which is costly. Cane also spoils quickly after cutting, so the mill belongs where the cane is cut.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: bulk-losing, because about seven tonnes of cane make one tonne of sugar; so the raw material is hauled the shortest distance; and cane spoils quickly, which causes the mill to sit in the fields.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows, for three industries in one country, the raw material needed for each tonne of finished product:

| industry | raw material per tonne of product |
|---|---|
| copper smelting | 45 tonnes |
| cement | 1.5 tonnes |
| bread baking | 0.9 tonnes |

Describe what the table suggests about where each industry tends to locate.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the raw-material weight falling from copper smelting (45 tonnes) to cement (1.5) to bread (0.9), and location tends to follow it. Copper smelting sits at the mine, because hauling 45 tonnes of ore for each tonne of metal would be costly, so the discarded mass stays at the pit. Cement sits at the quarry, which its 1.5 tonnes still favour. Bread sits in the market town: at 0.9 tonnes the flour weighs little more than the loaves, and because loaves go stale, the bakery belongs near the buyers. The gap is wide - 45 / 1.5 = 30, so copper smelting is about thirty times more tied to its raw material than cement.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - raw-material weight falls from copper to cement to bread (1 mark).

Values: the trend linked to location, because the figures explain the pull toward mine, quarry or market, so the most raw-material-tied industry is identified with its figure (1 mark); the comparison made explicit - 45 / 1.5 = 30 - which means the scale of the contrast is used (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Asked why a cement factory was built beside a quarry, a learner writes: "It creates jobs for local people, and the lorries bring noise and dust." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has answered a different question: the jobs, noise and dust are what the factory does once it is there - its impacts - not why it is located there. The correct answer gives location factors: the raw material sits in the quarry, cement is bulk-losing so haulage of rock is minimised, and the site is served by road or rail. The test is whether the answer says why here, or what happens here.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - impacts are not the same as location factors, and the question asked why the factory is located there.
1 mark: the correct idea - location factors such as the nearby raw material, transport and labour, instead of impacts.

items.prompt: Asked for a case study of an industrial zone, a learner begins: "I will write about Japan, because it is one of the most industrial countries in the world." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: A whole country is the wrong scale for an industrial case study: it cannot be marked on a town map, and it is too large for place-specific detail such as named estates, sites and figures. The correct choice is a named zone or factory - a cement works near Otavi, or an industrial estate on the edge of a city - small enough for real detail at one place. The test is whether the example could be marked on a town map.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - a country is not an industrial zone, and in fact the scale is wrong for place-specific detail.
1 mark: the correct idea - a named factory or zone is used instead, at a scale small enough to mark on a town map.

items.prompt: A bakery chain must choose between Site A beside the flour mill and Site B, 80 kilometres away in the main shopping town where most customers live. Suggest which site the chain should choose, and justify your decision.
items.canonical_answer: Site B, the market town, is the better choice. Flour is compact and keeps for weeks, so hauling it 80 kilometres is cheap, whereas loaves are bulky and go stale within a day, which means baking near the buyers cuts both delivery journeys and unsold bread. The judgement rests on the product's bulk: the baked goods are harder to carry than the flour they came from, so the factory belongs at the market end.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision between the two sites (1 mark).
Because the reasons are linked to the product's bulk and perishability, so the 80-kilometre distance and the daily deliveries both matter (1 mark).
Evidence: the bulk-gaining logic developed as the deciding point, which justifies the choice rather than asserting it (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For the Ohorongo cement works in northern Namibia, describe two features of its location.
items.canonical_answer: The works stands beside Otavi, a town on the north-south railway of the Otjozondjupa region, with its raw material at hand: the marble-rich rock is cut at a quarry beside the works. It is also placed in the heart of northern Namibia's building market, so the cement travels shorter distances to the construction sites that use it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all, each a fact about the named case study - the site near Otavi with its quarry, or the rail and market position - not a general point about cement.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why the Ohorongo cement works was located near Otavi rather than at the coast.
items.canonical_answer: The raw material decided the broad location: cement-making is bulk-losing, because well over a tonne of quarried rock goes into each tonne of cement, so the works belongs at the quarry rather than hauling rock hundreds of kilometres. Otavi's railway junction provided the transport: fuel and equipment arrive by rail and cement leaves the same way, so the site had links in every direction without new building. Labour and services came from Otavi itself, because a town already on the line supplies workers, water and power. And the market sits close: northern Namibia's growing towns buy cement that is costly to carry far, so an inland works near its buyers keeps haulage of the finished product short.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each point tied to this example: the nearby raw material, because cement is bulk-losing; the rail junction at Otavi, so fuel in and cement out; labour and services from the town; the northern market, so haulage of the finished product stays short.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.3 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows the main links of the Ohorongo cement works:

| link | what it provides the works |
|---|---|
| the quarry beside the site | marble-rich rock for the kilns |
| the town of Otavi | workers, water and services |
| the north-south railway through Otavi | fuel in, cement out |
| the main road north | access to building sites and towns |

Describe the pattern the table shows and what it suggests about the works as an industrial system.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows a works surrounded by its inputs and routes: the quarry supplies the raw material, Otavi supplies labour, water and services, and the railway and road carry the flows in and out. Every link has a direction - the quarry and town feed inputs to the processes, while the railway and road carry outputs to the market - so the table reads as an industrial system drawn on a real place. That pattern suggests a works placed to keep each flow short, because raw material, workforce and market all lie within reach of one site.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - each link feeds the works or carries its outputs away (1 mark).

Values: the direction of each flow made explicit, so the links are sorted into inputs and outputs of the system, which means the table is read as a whole rather than listed (1 mark); the interpretation of what the pattern suggests about the location, with the example developed (1 mark).

items.prompt: For a named factory or industrial zone, describe its location and explain why it is located there. [7]
items.canonical_answer: The Ohorongo cement works stands beside Otavi in the Otjozondjupa region of northern Namibia, on the country's north-south railway, with its raw material cut at a quarry beside the site. Production began in 2011 after an investment of about N$2.5 billion, and the works employs around 300 permanent workers (2010s figure). The location follows the industry's economics. Cement is bulk-losing, because well over a tonne of rock enters the kilns for each tonne of cement that leaves, so the works sits where the rock is rather than hauling it. Otavi's railway junction provides the transport, so fuel and equipment arrive and cement leaves by rail, north to the towns of the region and south towards the coast. The town supplies labour, water and services without new building. And the market lies near: northern Namibia's building trade buys cement that is heavy and costly to carry far, so the works keeps its delivery journeys short. Each factor points the same way - raw material, transport and market all meet at Otavi.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about factories needing materials or transport, with no named example or only general points.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named factory or zone, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - the Ohorongo works, Otavi and its railway junction, the quarry beside the site, the 2011 opening, about N$2.5 billion and around 300 workers - covering the description and the reasons.

items.prompt:
A juice company is choosing a site for a bottling plant. The table shows four possible sites:

| site | distance to orchards / km | distance to city market / km | distance to motorway / km | workforce within 10 km |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2 | 90 | 30 | 300 |
| B | 45 | 12 | 5 | 250 000 |
| C | 60 | 10 | 4 | 400 000 |
| D | 25 | 55 | 20 | 4 000 |

(a) Identify the site closest to the raw material. [1]
(b) Describe two features of Site D shown by the table. [2]
(c) Compare sites B and C as locations for the bottling plant, using figures from the table. [3]
(d) Suggest why the company might still prefer Site A despite its small local workforce. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Site A.
(b) Site D is middling on every link: 25 km from the orchards and 55 km from the city market, with the motorway 20 km away, so it is neither beside its inputs nor beside its customers; and its local workforce is 4 000 people, far smaller than the two city sites' quarter-million or more.
(c) Both are market-facing: 12 km and 10 km from the city. C has the larger workforce, 400 000 against B's 250 000, and sits 1 km nearer the motorway, 5 - 4 = 1. B is the nearer to the orchards, 45 km against C's 60, a gap of 60 - 45 = 15, so B keeps a shorter fruit journey while C offers about 150 000 more workers within 10 km, 400 000 - 250 000 = 150 000.
(d) Juice bottling is bulk-losing, because much of the fruit's mass is peel, pulp and water discarded at pressing, so a plant beside the orchards hauls less raw fruit; and a small workforce could be bussed in or housed at the site.
marking_guidance: Resource: parts (a) and (b) are read from the table - 1 mark for Site A; 2 marks for two features of Site D taken from the figures shown.
Marks: part (c) is worth 3 marks - the comparison needs paired figures from the table for workforce, market, motorway and orchards, with comparative terms backed by values.
Figures: part (d) is worth 2 marks - the reason must rest on bulk or perishability with the evidence of the site's distances, not a general preference for rural sites.
